Indexes speed up database queries by providing a data structure—often a B-tree—that allows the database to locate rows much faster than by scanning the entire table. Instead of checking every record sequentially, the database can navigate the index to jump directly to the relevant data, reducing the number of disk reads required.

However, indexes hurt performance in several scenarios. They consume additional disk space and require extra maintenance during data modification operations like inserts, updates, and deletes, as the index must be kept synchronized with the table. For very small tables or queries that return a large percentage of the rows, the overhead of maintaining and scanning the index can outweigh the benefit of a faster lookup. Additionally, excessive indexing can slow down write-heavy workloads and increase memory usage.

In autoregressive generation, a transformer predicts the next token one at a time. Without a cache, each new token requires recomputing the key and value (K and V) tensors for every previous token in the sequence. This is computationally expensive because the model must re-process the entire history for every single step.

The KV cache solves this by storing the K and V tensors from all previously processed tokens. When generating the next token, the model only computes the new token's K and V, then appends them to the cache. The attention mechanism then uses this stored history to attend to the full context without recalculating the old parts.

This reduces the per-step computation from a full re-evaluation of the sequence to a much smaller incremental update, making generation significantly faster and more efficient.

Optimistic locking assumes that conflicts are rare, so it doesn't lock data during a transaction. Instead, it checks for conflicts at commit time—often using a version number or timestamp. If the data has changed since it was read, the transaction fails and must be retried. This is efficient for read-heavy workloads with low contention, such as a social media feed where many users view posts but few edit them simultaneously.

Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely, so it locks the data as soon as it is read or modified. This prevents other transactions from accessing the data until the lock is released. It is safer for high-contention scenarios, like an inventory system where multiple users might try to buy the last item at the same time.

TCP congestion control responds to packet loss and latency by adjusting its sending rate to match the available network capacity. When packet loss occurs, TCP interprets it as a sign of congestion and reduces its sending rate, often by cutting the congestion window in half. This is typically handled through mechanisms like slow start, congestion avoidance, and fast retransmit/fast recovery.

Latency is managed through round-trip time (RTT) measurements. TCP uses these measurements to estimate how long it takes for data to travel to the receiver and back. If latency increases, it suggests the network is becoming congested or overloaded. TCP uses this feedback to adjust its sending rate, ensuring it does not overwhelm the network while still maintaining a high throughput.

In summary, TCP uses packet loss as a primary signal to back off and reduce its rate, while latency provides a secondary signal to gauge network health and adjust its sending behavior accordingly.
